findings: KEY DISCRIMINATOR RESOLVED: the guard is on the input BYTE INDEX (i > 0), not on whether the output buffer is empty and not on whether the previous char was a separator. Proof: "_A" -> "__a" (an output-empty rule would give "_a"; a previous-char-is-separator rule would also give "_a"). Corroborated by "-A" -> "-_a", " A" -> " _a", "__A" -> "___a", "_AB" -> "__a_b", "_A_" -> "__a_".

No collapsing/dedup of underscores whatsoever: "A_B" -> "a__b", "a_B" -> "a__b", "A__B" -> "a___b", "Already_Underscored" -> "already__underscored", "Ab_Cd_Ef" -> "ab__cd__ef". Already-lowercase snake_case is a fixed point: "already_underscored" -> "already_underscored".

Exhaustive single-byte sweep: probed "x<b>x" for every byte value b in 1..255 and dumped the output with od -tx1. EXACTLY bytes 0x41-0x5A ('A'-'Z') produced "x_<lower>x"; all 229 other byte values (0x01-0x40, 0x5B-0x7F, and every high byte 0x80-0xFF) were copied through unchanged. Byte 0x00 is unreachable via argv. This proves the classifier is plain ASCII isupper with the C locale and that high bytes are never treated as uppercase (no sign-extension surprise).

Non-ASCII UTF-8 passes through byte-for-byte (verified with od -tx1c): "Café" -> c3 a9 preserved -> "café"; "ÉCOLE" -> c3 89 5f 63 5f 6f 5f 6c 5f 65 (the É is untouched, and the following ASCII 'C' at byte index 2 DOES get a leading '_'); "日本語A" -> e6 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e 5f 61; "ÄÖÜ" -> unchanged c3 84 c3 96 c3 9c; "straße" -> unchanged. Invalid UTF-8 also passes through: "\xffZ" -> ff 5f 7a, "\xc3A" (lone lead byte) -> c3 5f 61.

Digits are ordinary pass-through bytes; underscores near digits come only from an adjacent capital: "A1B"->"a1_b", "a1B"->"a1_b", "1A"->"1_a", "99Test"->"99_test", "Test99"->"test99", "camelCase99Test"->"camel_case99_test".

Punctuation/whitespace are pure pass-through: "A-B"->"a-_b", "A.B"->"a._b", "A/B"->"a/_b", "A::B"->"a::_b", "A B"->"a _b", "A+B"->"a+_b", "A~B"->"a~_b", "A\tB"->"a\t_b", "A\nB"->"a\n_b" (verified via od, the embedded newline survives), "Hello World"->"hello _world", "hello-world"->"hello-world" (unchanged), "MyModule::MyClass"->"my_module::_my_class", "ActiveRecord::Errors"->"active_record::_errors". Notably it does NOT convert '::' to '/'.

Acronyms get one underscore per capital, no grouping: "ABC"->"a_b_c", "ABCD"->"a_b_c_d", "ABCDE"->"a_b_c_d_e", "HTMLParser"->"h_t_m_l_parser", "XMLHttpRequest"->"x_m_l_http_request", "getHTTPResponse"->"get_h_t_t_p_response", "SSLError"->"s_s_l_error", "ABCd"->"a_b_cd", "AbC"->"ab_c", "iOS"->"i_o_s", "IOs"->"i_os".
Empty string -> empty string (exit 0, verified with od: output line is just \n). Single chars: "A"->"a", "a"->"a", "Z"->"z", "z"->"z", "_"->"_", "__"->"__".
Long input has no truncation or limit. "AbC" x2000 (6000 bytes) -> 9999 bytes, exactly matching 4 + 1999*5. "A" x5000 -> 9999 bytes = 1 + 4999*2. Prefix/suffix spot-checks match.

Function is pure and stateless: no dictionary/irregular-word involvement. "Person"->"person", "Children"->"children", "Mice"->"mice", "Data"->"data", "Series"->"series", "Index"->"index", "Analyses"->"analyses" (all just a lowercased first letter). Passing the same word at argv[2] and argv[4] in one run gives identical output both times.

Driver line mapping CONFIRMED: underscore is emitted only for even argv indices (i%2==0), i.e. argv[2] and argv[4]. With 5 args the 15 output lines are: 1-2 = plural/camel(argv1), 3-5 = plural/camel/UNDERSCORE(argv2), 6-7 = plural/camel(argv3), 8-10 = plural/camel/UNDERSCORE(argv4), 11-12 = plural/camel(argv5), 13 = isPlural(argv1), 14 = isSingular(argv1), 15 = demodulize. With 4 args there are 13 lines (underscore at 5 and 10). A 6th argument is ignored entirely (i <= 5 cap). No args -> no output, exit 0.
Randomized differential test: 300 random strings over the alphabet [ABCXYZabcxyz0189_-.:/ ] (length 1-12) compared against the reference implementation above -> 0 mismatches.
All probes exited with status 0; nothing was ever written to stderr.

uncertainties: Byte 0x00 cannot be delivered through argv, so the behavior of a NUL byte inside the string is untestable via this driver. Given that all 255 other byte values follow the single rule and the function clearly iterates by size() rather than by C-string terminator (embedded 0x0A and 0xFF are handled fine), a 0x00 would almost certainly be copied verbatim as a non-uppercase byte — but this is inference, not measurement.

Whether the implementation literally calls std::toupper/std::tolower/std::isupper or does an inline range compare with +0x20 is indistinguishable black-box, because in the "C" locale they agree on every one of the 255 testable byte values. The observable mapping is exactly: 0x41-0x5A -> '_' + (byte+0x20) (with the leading '_' suppressed at index 0), everything else identity.
Whether the '_' + lowercase is produced by two separate appends or by appending a 2-char string is unobservable and irrelevant to the byte output.

Untested: inputs larger than ~6 KB were exercised (up to 5000 and 6000 bytes with correct lengths), but no multi-megabyte input was tried, so a pathological reallocation/limit above that size is not formally excluded (no evidence of any limit).

findings: 0 args (argc==1): completely empty stdout (0 bytes), empty stderr, exit 0. Inflector::initialize() prints nothing.
Loop guard `i < argc && i <= 5` confirmed: with 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 200 arguments the output is byte-identical to the 5-arg case; args 6+ are ignored entirely.
underscore() is emitted only for i==2 and i==4 (even i within 1..5). Verified: N=1 has no underscore line, N=2 has one (after arg2's camelize), N=3 still one, N=4 has two, N=5 still two.
Line-count formula confirmed empirically for argc-1 = 0..10: 0,5,8,10,13,15,15,15,15,15,15 == 2N+floor(N/2)+3 for N=min(argc-1,5)>=1, 0 for N=0.

Ordering confirmed: the whole results vector (all pluralize/camelize/underscore lines, interleaved per-argument) is printed BEFORE the three trailing lines. The trailing lines always refer to argv[1] only, never to the last arg.
Booleans print as the single bytes '0' and '1' (no std::boolalpha). E.g. `boxes` -> isPlural=1, isSingular=0; `people` -> 0,1.
Everything goes to stdout. `test15_executable cat 2>/dev/null` prints the full 5 lines; `test15_executable cat 1>/dev/null` prints nothing; `2>&1 1>/dev/null` yields 0 bytes in the success case.
Trailing newline: od -c shows the last byte is \n for every non-empty output; 0-arg output is exactly 0 bytes (no lone newline).
Empty-string argument in position 1 CRASHES: demodulize("Module::") does substr(9) on a size-8 string -> std::out_of_range -> terminate -> SIGABRT, shell exit status 134, 'core dumped'.

Empty-string arguments in positions 2..5 are harmless: pluralize("")="", camelize("")="", underscore("")="" all emit empty lines, exit 0. Verified with `x ""` (8 lines, several blank) and with `"" "" ""` (crashes only because argv[1] is empty).

Crash is NOT limited to the empty string: any argv[1] ending in the byte ':' also crashes (":", "::", "x:", "a::", "y:") because the last ':' lands on the final index so rfind(':')+2 > size. "x::y" and "A::B::C" do not crash (they yield an empty demodulize line).

Buffered lines ARE flushed before the crash: `test15_executable "" a b c d e f` prints 14 lines (2 blanks for the empty arg1, blocks for a,b,c,d, then '0' and '1') and only then aborts. Same when stdout is a pipe (std::endl flushes each line).

Byte-exact crash stderr is 147 bytes: "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'\n  what():  basic_string::substr: __pos (which is 9) > this->size() (which is 8)\n" for argv[1]==""; the numbers scale as size = 8+len(argv[1]), pos = size+1.
Exit status decomposes as 128+6 = SIGABRT; the process really is killed by signal 6, not exiting with code 134.
No flag parsing at all: "-h", "--help", "-", "--", "-v", "--version" are inflected like ordinary words (e.g. "--help" -> "--helps" / "--help" / demodulize "-help").
Args containing spaces, tabs, newlines, semicolons, and glob chars are passed through verbatim; a newline inside an arg simply produces extra physical lines.
Very long args work: a 100,000-byte 'a' argument yields 300,007 bytes of output (pluralize len 100001, camelize len 100000, demodulize len 99999), exit 0 — no truncation, no length limit observed.
argv[0] is unused: running through a symlink named /tmp/weirdname produces identical output.
stdin is never read: `< /dev/null` and `echo hello |` give identical output; closing stdout (`>&-`) still exits 0.

Locale-independent: LC_ALL in {C, POSIX, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8} gives byte-identical output for "I", "i", "istanbul", "ImageURL". Turkish locale does NOT produce dotted/dotless I. Plain ASCII case mapping is safe for a Rust port.

Byte-level (not codepoint) processing confirmed: "ÉCOLE" (c3 89 43 4f 4c 45) -> underscore = c3 89 5f 63 5f 6f 5f 6c 5f 65 ("\xc3\x89_c_o_l_e"); "café" and "日本語" pass through unchanged; invalid UTF-8 (ff fe) is passed through and gets an 's' appended by pluralize.

uncertainties: The exact classification of the crash exit status depends on the caller: the process dies from SIGABRT (signal 6). A POSIX shell reports 134; a Rust harness using std::process would see ExitStatus::signal() == Some(6) and code() == None. A Rust port that does not throw would need an explicit choice here.

The abort message text ('terminate called after throwing an instance of ...' plus the libstdc++ substr wording, including the two spaces after 'what():') is libstdc++-specific. A Rust port cannot reproduce it verbatim unless hard-coded; only the numbers (pos = 9 + len(argv[1]), size = 8 + len(argv[1])) are derived from the input.
I did not test an argument list large enough to hit ARG_MAX, nor stdout on a full filesystem / EPIPE mid-stream (SIGPIPE behavior on a closed pipe reader was not probed).

Whether the results vector is flushed all at once vs per-line is unobservable beyond what std::endl guarantees; every line is individually flushed, which is why partial output survives the abort. I could not distinguish 'vector then loop' from 'immediate print' by output alone — only by the fact that ordering is strictly results-then-trailing-block, which both models predict.

The per-function semantics (pluralize/camelize/underscore/isPlural/isSingular/demodulize) shown in the goldens are incidental to this dimension; other dimensions own their exact rules. I only verified enough to anchor line positions (notably that demodulize == s.substr(s.rfind(':')+2) on "Module::"+argv[1], which is what causes the crash).

findings: Only the byte '_' (0x5F) is a word separator. Exhaustive scan of camelize("a" + b + "b") for every byte b in 0x21..0x7E plus 0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20,0x7F and all of 0x80..0xFF: the output equals the input verbatim for every b except 0x5F, which yields "aB".

Exhaustive scan of camelize("x_" + b + "y") for every byte b: only b in 'a'..'z' (0x61..0x7A) is changed, and it is changed to b-0x20. Digits ('a_1'->'a1'), symbols ('a_-b'->'a-b', 'a_.b'->'a.b', 'a_/b'->'a/b', 'a_:b'->'a:b'), space ('a_ b'->'a b'), tab ('a_\tb'->'a\tb'), already-uppercase ('a_B'->'aB'), 0x7F, and every byte 0x80..0xFF pass through byte-for-byte unchanged. This proves ASCII-only std::toupper ("C" locale) with no Latin-1/locale mapping.

The capitalize flag is cleared by ANY consumed byte, not only by a letter. Discriminating input: "a_\tb" -> "a\tb" (byte-loop model), NOT "a\tB" (which a 'skip until first letter' model would produce). Likewise "a_-b" -> "a-b" and "_ _a" -> " A".

Runs of underscores collapse: 'a___b'->'aB', 'a__b'->'aB', '__a__b__'->'AB'. Leading underscores capitalize the first surviving byte: '___a'->'A', '_hello'->'Hello', '_ABC'->'ABC', '_x_y_z_'->'XYZ'. Trailing underscores emit nothing: 'a___'->'a', 'a_b_'->'aB'. All-underscore input returns the empty string ('_', '__', '___', '____', and 20000 underscores all -> "").

camelize never lowercases anything. The first byte is emitted verbatim unless it was preceded by '_': 'Hello'->'Hello', 'HELLO'->'HELLO', 'Hello_World'->'HelloWorld', 'ABC_DEF'->'ABCDEF', 'ONE_two_THREE'->'ONETwoTHREE', 'aBc_dEf'->'aBcDEf', 'camelCase_test'->'camelCaseTest', 'Foo__Bar'->'FooBar', 'A_b'->'AB'.

No Rails-style special handling of '/' or '::'. 'active_record/errors' -> 'activeRecord/errors', 'a_b/c_d' -> 'aB/cD', 'a_b::c_d' -> 'aB::cD', 'Module::foo_bar' -> 'Module::fooBar'. '/' is NOT converted to '::' and ':' is not a separator.

Whitespace is never trimmed and never acts as a separator: '  a_b  ' -> '  aB  ', ' _a' -> ' A', 'a_ ' -> 'a '. Newlines pass through literally (camelize("a
b") == "a
b", camelize("_
a") == "
a" — the '
' consumes the capitalize flag and is emitted unchanged).

UTF-8 is handled as raw bytes with no multi-byte awareness: camelize('a_é') == 'a' 0xC3 0xA9 (the 0xC3 lead byte consumes the capitalize flag and is emitted unchanged); camelize('ünïcode_tëst') == 0xC3 0xBC 'n' 0xC3 0xAF 'code' 'T' 0xC3 0xAB 'st' (i.e. 'ünïcodeTëst') — the ASCII 't' after '_' is uppercased, no non-ASCII byte is ever altered.

uncertainties: Behavior on an embedded NUL byte (0x00) inside the string is untestable through argv; the driver builds std::string from a C string so a NUL can never reach camelize via this harness. A std::string-based loop would presumably treat 0x00 as an ordinary non-'_' byte, but this is unverified.

The internal implementation (explicit byte loop vs. split-on-'_' + capitalize-each-token-after-the-first) cannot be distinguished: both models agree on every input probed, including empty tokens from consecutive/leading/trailing underscores. The pseudocode above is behaviorally exact either way.

Only the "C" locale was exercised (no locale env manipulation was attempted). If the binary were run under a locale where std::toupper maps bytes >= 0x80, output could in principle differ; under the observed default environment no byte outside 0x61..0x7A is ever modified.

findings: CONFIRMED: demodulize(s) == s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2). Every one of ~660 probes (20 hand-picked discriminators + 601 randomized words over the alphabet {a,b,':','::',':::',x,Y,_,space,-,'é',q} + non-ASCII + long strings) matched this model exactly, with zero mismatches in both value and crash/no-crash.

RULED OUT (a) pos=rfind("::"); substr(pos+3): discriminator W="a:" -> input "Module::a:" (len 10). rfind("::")=6 -> substr(9)="a:" (no crash). OBSERVED: crash with __pos 11 > size 10, i.e. pos+2 where pos=9=rfind(':'). Second discriminator W="a:bc" -> input "Module::a:bc" (len 12): rfind("::")=6 -> substr(9)="a:bc"; OBSERVED "c" = substr(11) = rfind(':')=9 plus 2.

RULED OUT (b) pos=find("::"); substr(pos+3) and (d) pos=find(':'); substr(pos+3): both always give find pos=6 -> substr(9), which for W="A::B" (input "Module::A::B", len 12) predicts "::B". OBSERVED: empty string. Also they would never crash for non-empty W, yet W="a:"/"a::"/":" all crash.

RULED OUT (e)-style two-step forms such as s.substr(pos+1).substr(1): the exception message names a single substr with __pos measured against the FULL string length (W="" -> "__pos (which is 9) > this->size() (which is 8)"; a two-step form would report __pos 1 > size 0). So it is one substr call on the whole string.

CONFIRMED (c): pos = rfind(':') (single byte 0x3A), return substr(pos + 2). Verified independently by the crash arithmetic: for every crashing input the message is exactly '__pos (which is N+1) > this->size() (which is N)' with N = 8 + byte_len(W) — consistent with last colon at index N-1 and start = N+1.
The search target is a SINGLE ':' byte, not the digraph "::": W="a:bc" -> "c" (last colon at input index 9, single, preceded by 'a').
Skip is a uniform +2 regardless of what precedes the last colon: W="a:bc" -> "c" and W="a::bc" -> "c" (last colon at 9 vs 10, both +2).
Byte comparison is exact/unsigned: W="\xba\xbab" (0xBA = 0x3A|0x80) -> result bytes ba 62, i.e. the 0xBA bytes were NOT treated as colons (pos stayed at 7 from the "Module::" prefix).
Other punctuation is not a separator: W="a;b" -> ";b", W="a.b" -> ".b", W="a/b" -> "/b", W="a|b" -> "|b" (all just input[9..], pos=7).

No case folding, trimming, or any other transformation: W="FooBar" -> "ooBar", W="HTTPServer" -> "TTPServer", W="no_colons_here" -> "o_colons_here", W="a::b " -> " " (trailing space preserved), W="a\tb" -> "\tb".

CRASH CONDITION (exact): std::out_of_range is thrown iff the LAST BYTE of the input string is ':' (equivalently, for this driver, iff W is empty or W's last byte is ':'). All other inputs return normally, possibly the empty string. Verified over 601 random inputs: crash <=> input ends with ':' held in every case.

Result is a raw BYTE slice with no UTF-8 awareness. W="é" (c3 a9) -> input "Module::" + c3 a9 (len 10), pos=7, substr(9) = single byte a9 = a lone UTF-8 continuation byte => INVALID UTF-8 output. W="日本語" (e6 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e) -> substr(9) = 97 a5 e6 9c ac e8 aa 9e, starts with continuation byte 0x97 => INVALID UTF-8. W="🎉" (f0 9f 8e 89) -> 9f 8e 89 => INVALID UTF-8. W="ü" (c3 bc) -> bc. W="€" (e2 82 ac) -> 82 ac.
W="café" -> "afé" (61 66 c3 a9) which happens to stay valid UTF-8 — so validity is incidental, purely a function of where byte 9 lands.

Length arithmetic is in bytes, confirmed via crash message: W="é:" (3 bytes) -> '__pos (which is 12) > this->size() (which is 11)' = 8+3=11. W="日本語:" (10 bytes) -> 19 > 18. W = 100*'z' + ':' (101 bytes) -> 110 > 109.
Long inputs behave identically (no truncation/limits): W = 500*'A' -> 499-byte result; W = "Mod::" + 300*'B' -> 299-byte result of all 'B' (last colon at index 12, substr(14)).
stdout produced before the throw IS flushed (std::endl flushes): crashing runs still emit the first 4 lines (pluralize, camelize, isPlural, isSingular) before aborting.

The 'no colon anywhere' case is unreachable through this driver because "Module::" is always prepended, so it cannot be observed. If the source literally is `s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2)`, npos + 2 wraps to 1 and the C++ result would be s.substr(1) — which itself throws only for an empty s. A port only needs to be correct for inputs containing ':'.

uncertainties: The behavior when the input contains NO ':' at all is unobservable through this driver ("Module::" is always prepended). If the source is literally `s.substr(s.rfind(':') + 2)`, then npos+2 wraps to 1 and C++ would return s.substr(1) (throwing only for empty s). If instead there is a guard (`if (pos == npos) return s;`), the result would be s unchanged. I could not discriminate these. Recommendation for a port: only the has-colon path needs to be byte-exact; for the no-colon path pick a safe fallback (return the input unchanged) and document it, since no test can exercise it via this driver.

Cannot distinguish `rfind(':')` from `find_last_of(":")` / a manual reverse scan for byte 0x3A — they are behaviorally identical for a single-character needle, so this is a distinction without a difference.

Cannot distinguish `substr(pos + 2)` from `substr(pos + 1 + 1)` or from "take the suffix after the last colon then drop its first byte" — identical outputs AND identical crash set for all reachable inputs, except that the two-step form would report a different __pos in the exception text; the observed exception text matches the single-substr form, so the single-substr form is the one to port.
NUL bytes inside the string cannot be tested (execve/argv is NUL-terminated), so behavior for embedded 0x00 is unknown; a byte-faithful port will handle it naturally.

Whether the thrown exception type/message must be reproduced by a port is a policy question. A Rust port would presumably return Err/panic; the exact C++ stderr text and SIGABRT (status 134) are recorded in the goldens if byte-exact process behavior is required.

uncertainties: Whether the empty-string identity comes from an explicit `if (word.empty()) return word;` guard or from "" being a member of the uncountable container is not observable black-box; the behavior is identical either way.
The container type (std::set vs unordered_set vs vector+std::find) is unobservable; only exact-byte whole-string membership semantics were confirmed.
Whether Inflector::initialize() could register a different uncountable set under other conditions is untestable through this driver; the observed set is fixed at those 10 words.
A NUL byte (0x00) inside the word cannot be passed via argv, so that byte value is untested (all of 0x01-0xFF were tested and behave as plain bytes).
Only lengths up to 100000 bytes were probed; no allocation-failure path was exercised.
